opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the really interesting questions, because there's a tension. On one hand, you'd like abstractions that are just good descriptions of the world: compressive, general, things that capture the causal structure no matter what you happen to care about. On the other hand, the world is enormously rich, and there are infinitely many regularities you could pick up on. Most of them don't matter to you. The pattern of cracks in the ceiling is a perfectly good regularity, but you're never going to need it.

So I think of reward as a way of breaking the symmetry between all the possible abstractions you could form. It tells you which distinctions are worth making. If two states of the world lead to the same outcomes for what you care about, then maybe you don't need to distinguish them, and you can lump them together. If some small detail turns out to determine whether you succeed or fail, then that detail suddenly deserves a concept of its own, even if it's not salient perceptually.

That said, I'm a little wary of the purely reward-driven picture, where the only thing that shapes your representation is a scalar signal. It's a pretty impoverished signal, and it's sparse. If you learn your abstractions only from reward, you tend to get representations that are brittle and overfit to one task. When the goal changes even slightly, they don't transfer.

What I find more compelling is a kind of interplay. You build models of the world that are trying to be broadly predictive and compositional, things like programs or causal models. Then reward, or more generally the goals and tasks you face, acts as a pressure on which parts of that model you elaborate and which you leave coarse. It's a bit like how a library of abstractions grows in program synthesis. You don't invent every possible function. You invent the ones that keep showing up in the solutions to problems you actually needed to solve. The problems provide the pressure, and the compression gives you the generality.

So reward helps you decide where to spend your representational budget, but I don't think it should be the only thing deciding what the representation is. You want abstractions that are useful, but also true enough that they'll still be useful when the reward changes.

r001.rationale: The response says abstractions are shaped by goals and tasks, and that people develop concepts and functions that recur in problems they need to solve.

r002.rationale: It explains that the world contains many possible regularities and that reward breaks the symmetry among them, guiding which distinctions to keep and which states to lump together.

r003.rationale: The response discusses reward, outcomes, and which model parts to elaborate, but does not identify planning toward reward as a criterion for evaluating a hierarchy of abstractions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really interesting question, and it's one where my views have actually shifted a bit over the years. The classic reinforcement learning answer is that reward is the thing that tells you which abstractions matter: an abstraction is valuable to the extent that it helps you predict or obtain reward, and everything else is just noise you can throw away. There's something right about that. If you're an agent in a world, the world is overwhelmingly rich, and you need some principle for deciding which of the infinitely many ways of carving it up are worth your limited compute and memory. Reward is one very natural principle.

But I think reward is a surprisingly weak signal for learning abstractions, and I'll try to say why. Reward is typically sparse, it's delayed, and it's scalar. You get one number, maybe at the end of an episode, and you're supposed to use that to figure out which of the thousands of intermediate concepts you could have formed were the right ones. That's a very low-bandwidth channel. If you compare that to what a human child gets, or what a scientist gets, most of the structure they're learning isn't coming from reward at all. It's coming from the structure of the environment itself: regularities, things that co-occur, things that compose, things that repeat across tasks.

So the way I like to think about it, coming more from the program synthesis and library learning side, is that abstractions are valuable when they're reused. If you're solving a bunch of problems and you keep writing the same subroutine over and over, that's a signal that the subroutine is a good abstraction, and that signal doesn't depend on any one task's reward. It's more like a compression argument. The abstraction earns its keep by making the whole collection of solutions shorter. In DreamCoder, for example, the library grows by finding fragments that get reused across many programs, and that's almost entirely a structural signal rather than a reward signal.

Where reward comes in, I think, is upstream of that. Reward determines which problems you bother to solve in the first place. It determines the distribution of tasks. And the distribution of tasks determines which fragments end up getting reused. So reward shapes abstraction indirectly, by shaping what you spend your time on, rather than directly, by scoring each abstraction. I think that's actually a healthier picture, because it means the abstractions you learn can be robust across tasks instead of overfit to one particular reward function.

There's a second role for reward that I think is underappreciated, which is in pruning. You can have a model of the world that makes tons of distinctions, and most of those distinctions don't matter for anything you'll ever want to do. Reward can tell you which distinctions are decision-relevant. Two states that look different but lead to the same outcomes under every policy you care about can be collapsed. That's the bisimulation kind of idea, and I think it's a legitimate way reward tells you what to abstract away. But notice that's about removing structure, not discovering it.

And then the last thing I'd say is that I think the honest answer is probably that you need both, and the interesting question is how they interact. Pure unsupervised structure learning will happily learn a lot of abstractions that are elegant and useless. Pure reward-driven learning will learn abstractions that are useful for one thing and brittle everywhere else. The thing we actually want is something like: use the structure of the world to propose abstractions, and use the pattern of what you actually need to do, which reward reveals over time, to decide which of those proposals to keep and build on. I think the world model side and the reward side are different kinds of evidence, and a good learner is a kind of Bayesian that weighs them together rather than letting one dominate.

r001.rationale: The response says reward-driven abstractions may be useful for one task, but does not state that people often construct abstractions specifically for the problem at hand.

r002.rationale: It says structure learning alone can produce elegant but useless abstractions and that reward helps identify which distinctions matter, conveying that environmental structure alone does not determine which information to discard.

r003.rationale: The response discusses reward relevance and collapsing states, but does not identify planning toward reward as a criterion for evaluating a hierarchy of abstractions.

astra-6.text:
I think reward gives you a way of saying which distinctions in the world matter for what you’re trying to do. There are many ways to compress your observations, but a good compression isn’t necessarily a good abstraction for acting. You might discard something that’s visually very small but crucial to whether you succeed.

So, for example, if you’re navigating a building, the exact texture of the walls may not matter, but whether a door is locked does. The reward helps determine which of those details you need to preserve. And that’s about more than predicting the immediate reward: you need to preserve distinctions that affect what you can do later and the rewards you can eventually reach.

The interesting complication is that we want abstractions that transfer. If you learn an abstraction around one very narrow reward signal, you might throw away information that another task needs. So I think reward helps select useful abstractions, but the range of tasks you’re learning across matters enormously. Ideally, you discover structure that makes many different goals easier to achieve.

r001.rationale: It describes learning an abstraction around a narrow reward signal and says the relevant distinctions depend on the task, conveying task-specific abstraction.

r002.rationale: It says observations admit many possible compressions and reward helps select which information to preserve, showing environmental observations alone do not determine the abstraction.

r003.rationale: It says abstractions should preserve distinctions that affect later actions and eventual rewards, but does not identify planning toward reward as a criterion for evaluating a hierarchy of abstractions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reward signal gives you a way of asking which distinctions in the environment actually matter. There are enormously many things you could represent about what you observe, but only some of them help you predict the consequences of your actions and achieve your goals.

Imagine you're learning to navigate a building. The precise texture of the wallpaper might be irrelevant, while whether a door is locked is very important. A useful abstraction preserves that distinction and lets you ignore a lot of the visual detail.

But reward doesn't uniquely specify the abstraction. You still have to discover the structure that makes the task easier to learn and solve. And something that's irrelevant for one task might be essential for another. So I would think of reward as providing pressure toward useful abstractions, rather than as giving you a complete description of what those abstractions should be.

r002.rationale: It says reward does not uniquely specify an abstraction, but does not clearly state that environmental data alone underconstrains the choice to discard information.
